subject: Career
title: Skills Audit: What You Actually Know
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Skills Audit: What You Actually Know.

hook.text: She said she had no marketable skills. Then she listed: project management, data analysis, client relations.

buildup.text: Most people underestimate their skills because they take their daily competencies for granted.

discovery.text: A skills audit categorizes abilities into technical, interpersonal, and cognitive — then rates proficiency.

twist.text: Skills you find boring might be rare. The thing that's easy for you might be hard for others.

climax.text: Ask five colleagues: 'What do you come to me for?' Their answers reveal your hidden strengths.

punchline.text: You have more skills than you think. Map them to see.

quiz.question: Why do people underestimate their skills?
options: They take daily competencies for granted

details.summary: A skills audit systematically catalogs your hard skills, soft skills, and domain knowledge to reveal hidden strengths and transferable assets. Most people significantly underestimate the breadth of their capabilities until they perform one.
details.whyItMatters: Without an honest inventory, career changers either undervalue themselves or pursue retraining they do not actually need, wasting time and money.
takeaways: Divide skills into hard, soft, and domain-specific categories
Ask colleagues for blind-spot identification during the audit
Update your skills audit at least once per year for accuracy

faq.question: What is the simplest way to conduct a personal skills audit?
faq.answer: List every task you perform in a typical week, then categorize each as a hard skill, soft skill, or domain expertise. Next, rate your proficiency and enjoyment for each item. The overlap of high proficiency and high enjoyment reveals your strongest transferable assets.

faq.question: How do you identify skills you use unconsciously?
faq.answer: Ask five trusted colleagues or friends what they come to you for help with. Skills that feel effortless to you often represent your deepest competencies, and outside perspectives surface what self-reflection misses.
